title: GOD HAD ALREADY CHOSEN JACOB… SO WHY DID REBEKAH HELP HIM LIE TO HIS BLIND FATHER?
paragraphs: GOD HAD ALREADY CHOSEN JACOB… SO WHY DID REBEKAH HELP HIM LIE TO HIS BLIND FATHER?

The heartbreaking story of a mother who believed God's promise but tried to control its fulfillment—and how one family's deception reveals a truth about faith, fear, brokenness, and the grace of Jesus Christ.
There is something deeply disturbing about the story of Rebekah and Jacob.
Not simply because a son deceived his elderly, blind father.
Not simply because a mother prepared the disguise, cooked the meal, and instructed her son to lie.
But because God had already spoken.

Before Jacob ever entered the world, before Esau ever sold his birthright, before Isaac's eyesight failed, before Rebekah ever placed goatskins on her son's hands, God had already revealed something extraordinary about the future of her children.
And yet, when the moment came, Rebekah behaved as though God's promise might collapse unless she intervened.
Think about that.
A woman who had heard from God became a woman who helped orchestrate a deception.
A mother who knew the promise became a mother who manipulated the circumstances.
A family chosen to carry forward God's covenant became a family torn apart by favoritism, secrecy, fear, and betrayal.
And perhaps the most uncomfortable part of this entire story is that we may recognize ourselves in it.
Because sometimes we don't stop believing God exists.
We simply stop trusting Him to act without our interference.
Sometimes we pray for His will, then panic when His timing refuses to cooperate with ours.
Sometimes we believe His promises with our mouths while our decisions reveal how frightened we are that He might not come through.
And sometimes, without realizing it, we begin trying to accomplish something good through methods God never commanded.
But here is the question that should trouble every believer: If God has promised something, does our fear give us permission to manipulate how it happens?
To understand what happened inside Isaac's tent, we must first return to a much quieter place.
A woman praying over a pregnancy she could not understand.
Rebekah had struggled with infertility for years. Genesis 25:21 tells us that Isaac prayed to the LORD for his wife, and God answered.
But the pregnancy that followed was anything but peaceful.
The children struggled within her so intensely that she went to inquire of the LORD.
And God answered her.
Genesis 25:23 records these words in the King James Version:
“Two nations are in thy womb, and two manner of people shall be separated from thy bowels; and the one people shall be stronger than the other people; and the elder shall serve the younger.”
In the original Hebrew, the final words are:
וְרַב יַעֲבֹד צָעִיר
Ve-rav ya'avod tsa'ir.
Commonly understood in this context as, “And the older shall serve the younger.”

The Hebrew word rav can convey greatness or seniority, while tsa'ir refers to the younger or smaller one. The prophecy concerns two children who would also become two peoples. Its fulfillment extends beyond the personal relationship of Jacob and Esau into the history of their descendants.
This was not an ordinary prediction.
In the ancient world, the firstborn son normally occupied a position of special privilege. Yet God announced a reversal of the expected order.
The younger would have a remarkable place in His unfolding purpose.
Jacob had not yet performed a good deed.
Esau had not yet committed a wrong.
Neither child had earned the future being announced.
God's purpose was already at work.
Centuries later, Paul would reflect on this very event in Romans 9:10–12, emphasizing God's purpose in election rather than human works.
But notice something important.
God revealed the outcome. He did not command Rebekah to achieve it through deception.
Those are two very different things.
And confusing them can lead a believer into terrible decisions.
Years passed.
The boys grew.
Esau became a skillful hunter, a man of the field. Jacob became a quieter man, dwelling among the tents.
Then Genesis 25:28 reveals a sentence that helps explain the emotional disaster waiting ahead:
“And Isaac loved Esau, because he did eat of his venison: but Rebekah loved Jacob.”
Read that again.
Isaac loved Esau.
Rebekah loved Jacob.
The Bible does not say these parents loved only one child each. But it does expose a divided household marked by parental favoritism.
And favoritism rarely remains a private emotion.
Eventually, it becomes visible in decisions.
In conversations.
In loyalties.
In the way one child is defended while another is overlooked.
In the things a family refuses to discuss openly.
Isaac's preference for Esau and Rebekah's preference for Jacob created a dangerous environment in which each parent had a favored son.
And then came the day when Isaac believed his death might be near.
Genesis 27 describes him as old, with eyesight so poor that he could no longer see.
He called Esau and instructed him to hunt game, prepare the food he loved, and bring it to him so that he could bless him.
There was something solemn about this moment.
A father approaching the end of his life.
A son preparing a meal.
A blessing about to be spoken.
But Rebekah was listening.
The text does not tell us everything she thought.
It does not reveal every fear passing through her mind.
It does not explicitly say that she remembered the prophecy at that exact moment.
We must be careful not to turn our imagination into Scripture.
But we do know that Rebekah had received God's earlier revelation, and we know what she did next.
Instead of confronting Isaac openly, appealing to the divine promise, or entrusting the outcome to God, she called Jacob and gave him instructions.
She would prepare food.
Jacob would take it to Isaac.
He would present himself as Esau.
And he would receive the blessing intended for his brother.
It was a deliberate plan.
Not an accidental misunderstanding.
Not a harmless family trick.
A calculated deception.
And Jacob knew the danger.
But listen carefully to his objection.
In Genesis 27:11–12, Jacob worried that Esau was hairy while he was smooth-skinned. If his father touched him, Isaac might recognize the deception and bring a curse upon him rather than a blessing.
Jacob's immediate objection was not that lying to his father would be sinful.
It was that he might be discovered.
That distinction is painful.
Because there is a kind of conscience that asks, “Is this right before God?”
And there is another kind that asks, “What if I get caught?”
Those questions can sound similar when fear is speaking.
But they lead in very different directions.
Rebekah answered in Genesis 27:13:
“Upon me be thy curse, my son: only obey my voice, and go fetch me them.”
What a devastating sentence.
A mother willing to bear the consequences of a plan she should never have devised.
Perhaps she believed she was protecting the future God had promised.
Perhaps her favoritism had blinded her to the moral cost.
Perhaps she feared Isaac's blessing would establish Esau in a position contrary to what God had revealed.
Scripture does not identify one exclusive motive, and we should not pretend that it does.
But her actions are unmistakable.
Rebekah attempted to secure a promised blessing through deception.
And that is where her story begins to look painfully familiar.
Have you ever been so afraid of losing something that you began justifying behavior you once knew was wrong?
Have you ever told yourself that a small lie was necessary because the outcome was important?
Have you ever manipulated a conversation, concealed a fact, exaggerated a story, or pressured someone because you were terrified of what might happen if you simply trusted God with the truth?
Perhaps you wanted to protect your marriage.
Perhaps you wanted your child to succeed.
Perhaps you were afraid of losing your position, your reputation, your finances, or your future.
And somewhere inside your heart, a dangerous argument began forming.
“God knows why I'm doing this.”
“My intentions are good.”
“I just need to make sure everything works out.”
But good intentions do not transform dishonesty into obedience.
And believing that God has a purpose does not give us authority to violate His character.
Jacob followed his mother's instructions.
Rebekah dressed him in Esau's garments.
She covered his hands and the smooth part of his neck with the skins of young goats.
Then Jacob entered his father's presence.
Imagine the silence inside that tent.
An elderly father unable to see.
A son standing before him wearing another man's clothes.
The smell of prepared food.
The weight of a blessing.
And a lie waiting to be spoken.
Isaac asked who had come to him.
Jacob answered in Genesis 27:19:
“I am Esau thy firstborn.”
Five words.
Five words that reveal how far Jacob was willing to go.
He did not merely allow his father to misunderstand.
He directly claimed to be someone he was not.
Then Isaac became suspicious.
How had the hunt been completed so quickly?
Jacob answered:
“Because the LORD thy God brought it to me.” (Genesis 27:20, KJV)
This is one of the darkest moments in the account.
Jacob did not merely lie.
He invoked God's name to support his lie.
He made the LORD part of an explanation for something the LORD had not done.
And that should make us uncomfortable.
Because invoking God's name does not make a dishonest action holy.
A religious explanation does not automatically establish divine approval.
And saying “God told me” when He has not spoken is not spiritual confidence.
It is a dangerous misuse of His name.
Isaac remained uncertain.
The voice sounded like Jacob.
The hands felt like Esau.
Genesis 27:22 captures the contradiction:
“The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau.”
What a haunting picture.
A father trying to discern the truth through conflicting evidence.
A son whose voice betrayed his identity.
A disguise convincing enough to overcome suspicion.
And a blessing being obtained through fraud.
Eventually Isaac blessed Jacob.
Genesis 27:28–29 includes blessings of abundance, dominion, and the submission of peoples.
The blessing was spoken.
Jacob departed.
And soon afterward, Esau returned.
He prepared the meal.
He entered his father's presence.
He asked for the blessing.
And suddenly the truth began to emerge.
Genesis 27:33 says Isaac trembled exceedingly.
Esau cried out with an exceedingly great and bitter cry.
This was no longer merely a clever scheme that had succeeded.
It was a family breaking apart.
A father shaken.
A brother devastated.
A son exposed.
A mother whose plan would carry consequences far beyond the moment she had anticipated.
Esau pleaded for a blessing of his own.
And in Genesis 27:38, he wept.

We should not ignore Esau's earlier choices. Genesis 25:29–34 records that he sold his birthright to Jacob, and the passage concludes by saying he despised his birthright. Hebrews 12:16–17 later warns believers through Esau's example.
But Esau's failure did not excuse Jacob's deception.
One person's sin does not sanctify another person's sin.
Both truths can stand together.
Esau had treated his birthright with contempt.
Jacob had deceived his father to obtain the blessing.
And Rebekah had helped arrange the deception.
Nobody needed to be portrayed as innocent for the suffering to be real.
Then the consequences intensified.
Esau began planning to kill Jacob after Isaac's death.
Rebekah learned of the threat and urged Jacob to flee to her brother Laban.
The mother who wanted to secure her son's future now had to send him away.
She had helped him obtain the blessing.
But she could not keep him safely at home.
And here is one of the saddest details in the narrative.
Scripture never records Rebekah seeing Jacob again after his departure.
That does not prove they never reunited. The Bible simply does not tell us.
But the silence is sobering.
The very son she favored was now separated from her.
The blessing had been obtained, yet the household was fractured.
Sometimes we can get the outcome we wanted and still discover that our methods have wounded the people we love.
And this brings us back to the original question.
Why did Rebekah help Jacob deceive Isaac when God had already spoken?
The most responsible biblical answer is that Scripture shows us her actions but does not explicitly disclose her full inner reasoning.
Her knowledge of God's prophecy, her favoritism toward Jacob, and her determination to redirect Isaac's intended blessing all provide important context.
It is reasonable to understand her conduct as an attempt to secure Jacob's future through human intervention.
But it would go beyond Scripture to claim with certainty that fear alone, ambition alone, or unbelief alone explains everything she did.
Human hearts are often more complicated than that.
What we can say confidently is that Rebekah acted as though a promised future needed to be protected by a sinful strategy.
And Scripture never commands us to imitate her deception.
God's sovereignty did not make her dishonesty righteous.
God's promise did not make Jacob's lie acceptable.
And God's eventual faithfulness did not mean the family escaped the consequences of its actions.
There is an important distinction every Christian needs to understand.
God can accomplish His purposes despite human sin.
That does not mean human sin becomes part of our moral duty.
Romans 3:8 rejects the idea of doing evil so that good may result.
God's ability to redeem evil never gives us permission to practice it.
And yet the story does not end with the broken family.
Because the God who spoke before the twins were born had not abandoned His covenant.
Jacob fled.
And on his journey, in Genesis 28, he dreamed of a stairway or ladder connecting earth and heaven, with angels ascending and descending.
There, God reaffirmed the promises associated with Abraham and Isaac.
The land.
The descendants.
The blessing that would reach the families of the earth.
And in Genesis 28:15, the LORD told Jacob:
“And, behold, I am with thee, and will keep thee in all places whither thou goest.”
Notice what this does not mean.
It does not mean God approved of Jacob's lies.
It does not mean deception had become a virtue.
It means God's covenant faithfulness was greater than Jacob's moral failure.
Jacob still had a long road ahead.
He would experience deception himself in Laban's household.
He would wrestle with fear, conflict, and the consequences of his earlier choices.
He would eventually face the terrifying prospect of meeting Esau again.
And in Genesis 32, Jacob would wrestle through the night and receive the name Israel.
The Hebrew name יִשְׂרָאֵל (Yisra'el) is connected in the narrative with striving or struggling with God, as Genesis 32:28 explains.
The man who once grasped for blessing through deception would come to a place where he clung to God and pleaded for blessing.
There is a profound movement in Jacob's story.
Not from a good man to a better man.
But from a deeply flawed man toward a life increasingly confronted, humbled, and shaped by God.
And when Jacob finally met Esau again in Genesis 33, something remarkable happened.
Esau ran to meet him.
He embraced him.
He fell on his neck and kissed him.
And they wept.
The brother Jacob feared had come to kill him instead welcomed him.
The text does not tell us that every wound disappeared or that their relationship became perfect.
But it records a reunion marked by unexpected mercy.
A family once torn apart by deception experienced a moment of reconciliation.
And perhaps someone reading this needs to hear that.
Your sin may have caused real damage.
Your decisions may have wounded people who trusted you.
You may have spent years living with consequences you cannot undo.
But repentance is still possible.
Humility is still possible.
Seeking forgiveness is still possible.
And God is still able to work in lives that have been deeply broken.
That does not guarantee every relationship will be restored exactly as it was.
It does not erase responsibility.
But it means your failure does not have to be the final word over your life.
And now we come to the deepest truth in this entire account.
The story of Rebekah and Jacob is not merely about a family that needed better communication.
It belongs to the larger story of God's covenant promise—a promise that ultimately leads us to Jesus Christ.
God had promised Abraham that through his offspring all the nations of the earth would be blessed.
That covenant continued through Isaac and Jacob.
And generations later, the Messiah came through the family line of Israel.
Matthew 1:2 begins tracing that line:
“Abraham begat Isaac; and Isaac begat Jacob; and Jacob begat Judas and his brethren.”
The Savior entered a family history that included favoritism, deception, rivalry, jealousy, suffering, and profound human weakness.
Yet the promise endured.
Not because every generation was faithful.
But because God was faithful.
And here is where the contrast becomes breathtaking.
Jacob entered his father's presence wearing the clothes of his brother.
He claimed an identity that was not his.
He sought a blessing through deception.
But Jesus Christ came into the world without deceit.
First Peter 2:22 says of Him:
“Who did no sin, neither was guile found in his mouth.”
Jacob lied to obtain a blessing.
Jesus spoke the truth even when it led Him toward the cross.
Jacob's deception fractured his family.
Jesus gave Himself to reconcile sinners to God.
Jacob sought blessing for himself.
Jesus bore the curse of the law to redeem those who trust in Him.
Galatians 3:13 declares:
“Christ hath redeemed us from the curse of the law, being made a curse for us.”
Do you see the beauty of the Gospel?
We do not need to disguise ourselves as someone else to be accepted by God.
We do not need to pretend our record is clean.
We do not need to manufacture a false identity or hide our history behind religious appearances.
We come to God through Jesus Christ, who is perfectly righteous and who gave Himself for sinners.
Second Corinthians 5:21 says:
“For he hath made him to be sin for us, who knew no sin; that we might be made the righteousness of God in him.”
This does not mean God simply overlooks evil.
It means our forgiveness rests upon the saving work of Christ.
The cross reveals both the seriousness of sin and the astonishing mercy of God.
Jesus did not die because our deception was harmless.
He died because sin is serious enough to require redemption, and His love is great enough to provide it.
And this is where Rebekah's story stops being merely ancient history.
Because there may be a Rebekah-like struggle inside your own heart.
You believe God.
But you are terrified of waiting.
You know what Scripture says.
But you are tempted to take control.
You want a blessed future.
But you are considering a dishonest shortcut.
You want your children to succeed.
But you are tempted to manipulate their circumstances.
You want your marriage to survive.
But you are hiding things that need to be brought into the light.
You want financial security.
But you are tempted to compromise your integrity.
You want God to open a door.
But you keep reaching for the handle of a door He has not opened.
And maybe the hardest thing God is asking of you right now is not to do more.
Maybe it is to stop doing what you already know is wrong.
To tell the truth.
To confess what you have concealed.
To release what you cannot control.
To trust Him enough to obey even when obedience feels frightening.
Proverbs 3:5–6 says:
“Trust in the LORD with all thine heart; and lean not unto thine own understanding. In all thy ways acknowledge him, and he shall direct thy paths.”
The Hebrew verb בְּטַח (batach), translated “trust,” conveys reliance or confidence.
Biblical trust is not merely agreeing that God exists.
It is resting our confidence in Him rather than treating our own understanding as ultimate.
That does not mean we become passive or refuse to make responsible decisions.
It means our actions must remain consistent with God's revealed will.
Faith is not permission to do nothing. But neither is faith permission to do wrong in order to get something right.
And perhaps that is the truth Rebekah's story was waiting to teach us.
You cannot improve God's righteousness by adding your dishonesty.
You cannot protect His promises by violating His commands.
You cannot make manipulation holy by calling it faith.
But when you have already failed, you can still come to Him in repentance.
You can confess.
You can turn away from deception.
You can begin making things right where possible.
And you can trust the Savior who welcomes repentant sinners.
First John 1:9 gives this promise:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
Maybe you have spent years pretending to be someone you are not.
Strong when you are exhausted.
Faithful when you are secretly struggling.
Peaceful when your heart is full of fear.
Confident when you are terrified of losing control.
Maybe you have been wearing a disguise for so long that you barely remember what honesty before God feels like.
You do not have to bring that disguise into His presence.
He already knows.
He knows the compromises.
The hidden motives.
The prayers mixed with fear.
The mistakes you regret.
The people you have hurt.
The nights when you wondered whether your life had become too tangled for grace to reach you.
And still, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Repent.
Believe in Jesus Christ.
Come into the light.
Receive the forgiveness that only He can give.
Because the Christian hope is not that God will eventually discover we were good enough.
It is that Jesus Christ is sufficient to save those who come to God through Him.
And if this story has exposed something in your heart, please do not rush past that conviction.
Sit with it.
Pray over it.
Ask the Holy Spirit to reveal where fear has begun replacing trust.
Not to impress anyone.
Not to prove how spiritual you are.
But as a simple expression of the prayer your heart may need to pray.
Someone else may need to know that repentance and restoration are possible.
There may be a mother reading this who has been carrying guilt over decisions she made for her children.
A father who realizes his favoritism wounded his family.
A son or daughter still grieving the betrayal of someone they trusted.
A believer who knows the right promises but has been choosing the wrong methods.
Please hear this carefully.
The Gospel does not invite you to deny what happened.
It invites you to bring what happened to Jesus Christ.
Because He is not merely interested in improving your public image.
He came to save sinners and transform lives.
And that is why Gospel Warrior exists.
Not simply to publish Christian articles that people read and forget.
But to keep placing Scripture before hearts that need truth, encouragement, correction, repentance, healing, and a deeper understanding of Jesus Christ.
A single share may place this Scripture-centered message before a friend, a family member, a struggling believer, or someone who has never seriously considered the Gospel.
You may never know who needed to read it that day.
For those who want to help this ministry continue and grow, I also want to extend a personal invitation.
And Scripture teaches us that Christian giving should be willing, sincere, and free from coercion.
Second Corinthians 9:7 says:
“Every man according as he purposeth in his heart, so let him give; not grudgingly, or of necessity: for God loveth a cheerful giver.”
It is one practical way to participate in the mission if you believe in what this ministry is doing and are financially able to help.
It should be a genuine desire to see the truth of Jesus Christ shared faithfully.
The heart behind these resources is simple: to help people move beyond occasional inspiration into sustained biblical learning, spiritual nourishment, and a life increasingly shaped by God's Word.
You can still help by praying, commenting thoughtfully, sharing the article, inviting others to follow, and pointing people toward the free resources available.
Your financial circumstances do not determine your value before God.
What matters is faithfulness to Jesus Christ.
And as we close, I want to bring you back to that tent.
An old father.
A disguised son.
A mother trying to control a promised future.
A blessing spoken.
A family broken.
What began with God's promise became entangled in human fear.
But God did not surrender His redemptive purpose to the failures of that family.
The story continued.
Through Jacob.
Through Israel.
Through generations of imperfect people.
Until, in the fullness of time, Jesus Christ came.
The promised Savior.
The sinless Son.
The One who did not deceive His Father.
The One who obeyed even unto death.
The One who rose again.
The One who calls sinners out of hiding and into the light of His grace.
And perhaps that is the question you need to carry into your prayers tonight.
Are you trusting God's promise?
Or are you trying to force His hand?
Are you obeying His Word?
Or are you justifying something you know is wrong because you are afraid of what will happen if you stop?
The God who was faithful to His covenant despite Jacob's deception is still faithful today.
But His faithfulness is never an excuse for our disobedience.
It is the very reason we can repent, surrender, and trust Him.
So put down the disguise.
Tell the truth.
Confess the sin.
Release the outcome.
Trust the Savior.
And remember this:
You do not have to become someone else to receive the grace of Jesus Christ—you have to stop hiding from the One who already knows you and still calls you to come home.
